definition: A production technique that frees hydrocarbons trapped in the pore spaces of impermeable rock (shale) by fracturing the rock, typically by pumping water or another fluid underground and using pressure/compression waves to crack the formation so hydrocarbons can migrate to the surface.
core_idea: Unlike traditional drilling, which taps hydrocarbons already pooled in permeable reservoir rock under an impermeable cap, fracking manufactures permeability in rock where hydrocarbons are otherwise locked in place.
key_points: Traditional wells target reservoirs formed where migrating hydrocarbons are trapped under an impermeable rock layer.
Fracking targets hydrocarbons trapped directly inside impermeable rock (shale) rather than pooled reservoirs.
The rock must be fractured before hydrocarbons can flow, distinguishing it from conventional drilling.
Fractures are commonly created by injecting hydraulic fluid to propagate compression waves from explosions into the formation.
caveats: Fracking is not the same process as conventional drilling with an extra step; the underlying geology being targeted (hydrocarbons locked in impermeable rock vs. pooled in permeable rock) is different.
